# XC Flow Academy · Lab Guide & Component Reference

<!-- Generated by `npm run docs` from src/data/guides.js and src/data/reference.js. Do not edit by hand. -->

This guide explains how to run every lab in the simulator and what each F5 Distributed Cloud component does. The same content is built into the app: each lab has a **How to run this lab** panel above the console, and the **Component Reference** button in the header opens a searchable glossary.

## How the workbench works

Every module screen is split in two. On the left is the live architecture diagram with an inspector card; on the right is the simulated XC Console with one tab per lab.

1. Pick a module in the skill tree, then a lab tab above the console.
2. Read the lab guide panel: objective, steps and what success looks like.
3. Do the steps in the console. Wrong choices are explained inline, so experimenting is safe.
4. Stuck? Open **Hints**, and only then **Reveal solution**.
5. Watch the diagram react: sites come online, tunnels turn green, attacks die at the RE.

XP is awarded once per objective, so you can replay any lab. Labs that depend on earlier work (for example, a site being online) offer a **Fast-track (no XP)** button.

### Using the diagram

The diagram is live: it reacts to what you do in the console labs. Use the Flows buttons to animate traffic and the Layers buttons to reveal what is happening underneath. Click any box to open its inspector card.

| Control | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| North-South | Internet user → nearest RE (Anycast) → tunnel → CE → origin. Needs the on-prem site online to complete. |
| East-West | Service A in AWS → AWS CE → fabric → on-prem CE → Service B. Needs both AWS and on-prem sites online. |
| Attack Traffic | Malicious requests hitting the RE. They die at the WAAP shield when your security controls are on. |
| Control Plane | Dotted lines from the SaaS console to every site: config only, never user traffic. |
| Data Plane | The backbone and the paths user traffic actually takes. |
| Tunnel Status | Green = tunnel up, amber = provisioning, grey = down. |
| WAAP Enforcement | Shows the security shield in front of the RE. |
| RELT Telemetry | Live latency labels per edge. A red label is a problem edge. |

<a id="module-1"></a>
## Module 1: Platform Architecture & Core Components

F5 XC splits the platform into a centralized SaaS control and management plane and a distributed data plane. The data plane is made of F5-operated Regional Edges (REs) on the Global Private Network and Customer Edges (CEs) that you deploy into clouds and data centers. A CE registers with a token, then automatically builds redundant IPsec (SSL fallback) tunnels to the two nearest REs.

**Canvas exercises**

- **Inspect 3 architecture components** (+30 XP): Click any three components in the diagram (for example an RE, a CE and the SaaS console) and read their inspector cards.
- **Watch a North-South flow reach the on-prem origin** (+20 XP): Register the On-Prem site in the Site lab (or fast-track it), keep Data Plane on, and turn on North-South. Watch packets reach the origin.
- **Reveal the Control Plane layer on the canvas** (+20 XP): Click the Control Plane layer to reveal the config channel from the console to each site.

### 1.1 Site & Tunnel Registration

**Objective:** Admit two new Customer Edge sites (AWS and On-Prem) into your tenant and watch each one build two encrypted tunnels to its nearest Regional Edges.

**Steps**

1. Read the Pending registrations list. Each CE has booted with your site token and is waiting for approval.
2. Click Review & Accept on acme-aws-use1. Check the site name, certified hardware, coordinates and the two nearest REs.
3. Click Accept registration. Watch the six provisioning steps run: token check, node admission, software upgrade, tunnel to RE #1, tunnel to RE #2, online.
4. Repeat for acme-dc1-vmware (the on-prem site). Optional: tick "Corporate firewall blocks UDP 4500" first to see the SSL fallback.
5. Look at the Sites & tunnels section and the diagram: both tunnels per site should turn green.

**Success looks like:** Both sites show ONLINE with two tunnels UP each (IPsec, or SSL for on-prem if you ticked the firewall box). The canvas tunnels turn green.

**XP objectives:** Approve the AWS CE site registration (+60) · Approve the On-Prem CE site registration (+60) · Bring all CE→RE tunnels online (+40)

**Hints**

- A CE only connects outbound. You never open inbound ports or configure VPN peers by hand.
- Tunnels go to two different REs so one PoP can fail without an outage.
- You can decommission a site with the bin icon and register it again to practise.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

- Accept acme-aws-use1, then accept acme-dc1-vmware. Wait for each to reach ONLINE.

</details>

**Components used:** [Site Token & Registration](#ref-registration), [Customer Edge (CE)](#ref-ce), [IPsec / SSL Tunnels (CE ↔ RE)](#ref-tunnels), [Regional Edge (RE)](#ref-re), [Site](#ref-site)

### 1.2 GCP Cloud Site Deploy

**Objective:** Deploy a production-grade GCP cloud site that survives a zone outage and handles both inbound and outbound traffic for the checkout VPC.

**Steps**

1. Read the requirement banner: region, high availability, and inbound plus egress traffic.
2. Pick the cloud credentials XC will use to build the site.
3. Choose the GCP region where the checkout workloads live.
4. Pick the site type that has both an inside and an outside interface.
5. Choose the node count and availability zones for high availability.
6. Click Apply (deploy site). If validation fails, read each red message, fix it and apply again.

**Success looks like:** The deployment log runs from terraform plan to "Site ONLINE", and two IPsec tunnels show UP to the regional REs.

**XP objectives:** Deploy an HA GCP cloud CE site (+60)

**Hints**

- Cloud sites register themselves through your credentials, so there is no token to approve.
- A CE should sit in the same region as the workloads it fronts.
- Egress through the CE needs two interfaces. Surviving a node failure needs quorum.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

- Cloud credentials: gcp-acme-sa
- Region: asia-southeast1 (Singapore)
- Site type: Ingress/Egress Gateway (Two Interface)
- Nodes: 3, zones a, b and c all ticked

</details>

**Components used:** [Cloud Sites (AWS VPC, Azure VNet, GCP VPC)](#ref-cloud-site), [CE 3-Node Cluster (High Availability)](#ref-ce-cluster), [IPsec / SSL Tunnels (CE ↔ RE)](#ref-tunnels)

### 1.3 Namespace RBAC

**Objective:** Replace pilot-era "Admin on all namespaces" grants with least-privilege access: one role in one namespace per person.

**Steps**

1. Read each person's job description.
2. For each person, pick a role from the first drop-down.
3. Pick the namespace scope from the second drop-down.
4. Click Run access review. Red notes explain any wrong role or scope.

**Success looks like:** Every person shows a green check and the review passes.

**XP objectives:** Pass a least-privilege namespace access review (+60)

**Hints**

- system holds sites and networking, shared holds reusable security objects, acme-shop holds the app's LBs and pools.
- An auditor must not be able to change anything, but must see everything.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

- Priya: Developer in acme-shop
- Sam: Security Operator in shared
- Lee: Network Operator in system
- Kim: Monitor (read-only) in all namespaces

</details>

**Components used:** [Roles & RBAC](#ref-rbac), [Namespace](#ref-namespace)

### 1.4 CE Upgrade Lifecycle

**Objective:** Plan a CE fleet upgrade (software and OS) that never takes a production app offline.

**Steps**

1. Read the fleet: one staging CE, two 3-node clusters and one single-node on-prem site.
2. For each decision row, choose an option from the drop-down.
3. Click Execute upgrade plan. Any wrong decision is flagged with a hint.

**Success looks like:** The rollout log shows staging first, rolling clusters, the on-prem site drained in a window, and the OS upgrade in a second wave.

**XP objectives:** Plan a zero-downtime CE fleet upgrade (+60)

**Hints**

- Canary first, healthy sites only, one node at a time, one change at a time.
- A single-node site has no peer to take over while it reboots.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

- Which site first: acme-staging-ce
- Pre-upgrade check: confirm site health, both tunnels up, no alerts
- 3-node clusters: rolling, one node at a time
- Single-node on-prem: maintenance window after shifting its apps
- Order: software release first, verify, then OS

</details>

**Components used:** [CE Software & OS Upgrades](#ref-upgrade), [CE 3-Node Cluster (High Availability)](#ref-ce-cluster)

### 1.5 Azure VNet Site

**Objective:** Place a zone-redundant CE in an Azure hub-and-spoke network so all spoke VNets reach the XC fabric and the internet through it.

**Steps**

1. Read the scenario: one hub VNet, three app spoke VNets, no single point of failure.
2. Answer each decision: where the CE lives, site type, HA, how spokes route to it, and the NSG.
3. Click Deploy site and read any flagged rows.

**Success looks like:** The log shows 3 nodes in zones 1, 2 and 3, spoke route tables updated and tunnels UP to two REs.

**XP objectives:** Deploy a zone-redundant Azure hub CE (+60)

**Hints**

- Shared services belong in the hub.
- Without a route change, spokes keep using Azure's default internet path.
- The CE dials out to REs, so it needs no open inbound ports.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

- Where: in the hub VNet (new CE subnets)
- Site type: Ingress/Egress Gateway (Two Interface)
- HA: 3 nodes across availability zones 1, 2 and 3
- Spoke routing: UDR 0.0.0.0/0 → CE internal LB, or Azure Route Server (BGP). Either is correct.
- NSG: allow outbound UDP 4500 / TCP 443 to REs, no unsolicited inbound

</details>

**Components used:** [Cloud Sites (AWS VPC, Azure VNet, GCP VPC)](#ref-cloud-site), [CE 3-Node Cluster (High Availability)](#ref-ce-cluster), [IPsec / SSL Tunnels (CE ↔ RE)](#ref-tunnels)

### 1.6 Virtual Sites & Labels

**Objective:** Write label selectors for three virtual sites so each one matches exactly the right sites, now and in the future.

**Steps**

1. Read the labels on each of the five sites in the banner.
2. For each virtual site, choose the selector that matches only the intended sites.
3. Answer why virtual sites beat listing sites by name.
4. Click Evaluate selectors.

**Success looks like:** All selectors match the right sets and the run passes.

**XP objectives:** Target sites precisely with label selectors (+60)

**Hints**

- Check every selector against the staging site: it is in AWS and the US, but it is not production.
- A good selector still works when a new site is added.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

- eu-edge: env == prod AND geo in (eu)
- public-cloud-prod: env == prod AND cloud != onprem
- canary: env == staging
- Why: new sites with matching labels join automatically

</details>

**Components used:** [Virtual Site](#ref-vsite), [Site](#ref-site)

### 1.7 API Credentials & Automation

**Objective:** Give Terraform CI and a developer's vesctl access to XC without creating a long-lived, all-powerful key.

**Steps**

1. Read the two needs: a CI pipeline and a laptop script.
2. Choose the credential, role, type, expiry and storage for each.
3. Click Run pipeline and audit.

**Success looks like:** The audit passes: scoped service credential, short expiry with rotation, and no secret in Git.

**XP objectives:** Automate XC safely with scoped, expiring credentials (+60)

**Hints**

- Automation should not depend on one person's account.
- Least privilege and expiry apply to machines too.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

- CI credential: a service credential with its own role and namespaces
- Role: only the roles needed in system, shared and acme-shop
- Laptop: API certificate (p12) in the OS keychain
- Expiry: 90 days with automated rotation
- Storage: CI secret store, injected at run time

</details>

**Components used:** [API Credentials & Service Credentials](#ref-apicreds), [Roles & RBAC](#ref-rbac), [SaaS Control & Management Plane (XC Console)](#ref-console)
